title: How do you calculate payback and NPV in a case interview, step by step?
description: Worked examples of payback and simple NPV for investment cases, with discount factors to remember and how to explain the result.
hook: Investment cases often end with the question "is it worth it?" Payback gives a quick answer; NPV gives a better one. Here are both worked through with numbers you could do on paper.
body:
Payback

A new machine costs £1M and saves £300k a year. Payback = 1,000 ÷ 300 ≈ 3.3 years. If the client wants payback within four years, it passes.

Simple NPV

The same machine lasts five years, and the client's cost of capital is 10%. Discount factors to remember at 10%: year 1 ≈ 0.91, year 2 ≈ 0.83, year 3 ≈ 0.75, year 4 ≈ 0.68, year 5 ≈ 0.62. Together they add to about 3.79.

Present value of savings: £300k × 3.79 ≈ £1.14M. NPV = £1.14M − £1M = about +£140k. Positive, so the investment creates value.

When payback misleads

Project A pays back in 2 years but lasts 3. Project B pays back in 3 years but lasts 10. Payback prefers A; NPV will usually prefer B. Always compare payback with the asset's life.

How to say it

It pays back in just over three years, within the target, and over its five-year life it creates about £140k of value after allowing for a 10% cost of capital.

More background in the time value of money explained.

The fast payback answer can point in the wrong direction

A factory can purchase a machine for £1 million today. The machine generates £300,000 of incremental net cash flow at the end of each of the next five years. Simple payback is £1m ÷ £300k ≈ 3.3 years. It passes a four-year payback rule, but that says nothing about the time value of money or whether the project earns more than the firm's required return.

At a 10% discount rate, the five annual cash flows have a combined present-value factor of about 3.79. Their present value is £300,000 × 3.79 ≈ £1.137 million. Subtract the £1 million initial investment to get NPV ≈ +£137,000. Under these assumptions the project creates value; a negative NPV would mean it does not meet the 10% return requirement.

Do not confuse cash flow with accounting profit. Depreciation reduces reported profit but does not itself consume cash each year. A more realistic investment case includes taxes, maintenance, working capital, installation costs, any resale value and the risk that savings do not materialise. Keep the discount rate consistent with the risk and cash-flow definition.

Try it aloud: "The project pays back in about 3.3 years and has an estimated positive NPV of £137,000 at 10%. My main sensitivity would be the reliability of the £300,000 annual benefit." One calculation establishes affordability; the other tests value creation.
